bakhtin: Mikhail Bakhtin (1895–1975) was a Russian thinker who worked on language, the novel, and culture, often under hard Soviet conditions. He is best known for the idea that all speech is dialogic — answering and contested by other voices — and for celebrating the subversive, leveling energy of carnival, in which official hierarchies are briefly turned upside down.
carl-schmitt: Carl Schmitt (1888–1985) was a German political theorist famous for defining politics by the friend–enemy distinction and for arguing that sovereignty means deciding the state of exception when normal law is suspended. A brilliant and controversial figure, he joined the Nazi party, and his critique of liberalism still provokes fierce debate on both left and right.
charles-taylor: Charles Taylor (b. 1931) is a Canadian philosopher and one of the leading communitarian critics of liberal individualism. He argues that the self is formed through language, community, and what Hegel called the struggle for recognition, and he has written influentially on authenticity, secularization, and the moral sources of modern identity.
cicero: Cicero (106–43 BC) was a Roman statesman, orator, and lawyer who did more than anyone to bring Greek philosophy into Latin — and thus into Western thought. Drawing mostly on Stoicism and the skeptical Academy, he wrote influential works on duty, friendship, natural law, and the conditions of a just war, while defending the Roman Republic with his life.
foot: Philippa Foot (1920–2010) was a British moral philosopher who helped revive virtue ethics as a serious rival to utilitarianism and Kantian duty ethics. She invented the trolley problem to probe the difference between doing harm and allowing it, and later developed a naturalistic account of moral goodness in her book Natural Goodness.
galen-strawson: Galen Strawson (b. 1952) is a British analytic philosopher known for starkly argued positions on the self and free will. He defends the reality of the self against narrative theories of identity, and his 'Basic Argument' contends that no one can be truly responsible for their actions, since we cannot be causa sui — the cause of ourselves.
george-herbert-mead: George Herbert Mead (1863–1931) was an American pragmatist philosopher and social psychologist at the University of Chicago. He argued that the self is not innate but emerges through social interaction — especially by taking the perspective of others — a view that founded symbolic interactionism and reshaped ideas about identity, mind, and language.
gettier: Edmund Gettier (1927–2021) was an American philosopher famous for a single three-page paper. In 1963 he showed with counterexamples that knowledge cannot simply be justified true belief — cases exist where you have a justified true belief that is true only by luck. The 'Gettier problem' reorganized the whole field of epistemology.
giorgio-agamben: Giorgio Agamben (b. 1942) is an Italian philosopher who writes on law, power, and politics in the tradition of Heidegger and Foucault. He is best known for the figure of homo sacer and the concept of 'bare life': people stripped of political standing, exposed to sovereign power most starkly in the camp and the state of exception.
goldman: Alvin Goldman (b. 1938) is a leading American epistemologist. He proposed reliabilism, the view that a belief counts as knowledge when it is produced by a reliable process such as perception or good reasoning, a move that shifted epistemology from inner justification to the causes of belief. He also pioneered the study of social epistemology.
haraway: Donna Haraway (b. 1944) is an American feminist theorist of science and technology. Her 'Cyborg Manifesto' uses the figure of the human–animal–machine hybrid to dissolve rigid boundary concepts like nature versus culture, and her notion of 'situated knowledges' argues that all knowledge is partial and located, never from a neutral god's-eye view.
john-hick: John Hick (1922–2012) was a British philosopher of religion known for two big ideas: a 'soul-making' theodicy, on which evil and suffering exist because a world that builds moral and spiritual character is more valuable than a ready-made paradise, and a pluralism holding that the major world faiths are different culturally shaped responses to one ultimate divine reality.
joseph-campbell: Joseph Campbell (1904–1987) was an American comparative mythologist who drew on Jung's archetypes to argue that the world's myths share one underlying pattern, which he called the monomyth or 'hero's journey' — departure, initiation, and return. His book The Hero with a Thousand Faces became a template for screenwriters and students of storytelling alike.
mackie: J. L. Mackie (1917–1981) was an Australian philosopher who taught at Oxford, known for hard-headed atheism and moral skepticism. In The Miracle of Theism he argued that the problem of evil makes belief in an all-good, all-powerful God irrational, and in Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong he defended 'error theory' — that objective moral values do not exist.
max-weber: Max Weber (1864–1920) was a German sociologist and political economist, one of the founders of modern social science. His Protestant Ethic thesis traced capitalism's roots to religious ideas, and he analyzed how modernity 'disenchants' the world and how states claim legitimate authority. His debates with Marxist historical materialism shaped twentieth-century social theory.
mctaggart: J. M. E. McTaggart (1866–1925) was a British idealist philosopher at Cambridge who gave the modern philosophy of time its basic vocabulary: the A-series of past, present, and future, and the B-series of earlier and later. Famously, he argued that time itself is unreal — that the two series contradict each other — a paper that still drives debates today.
milton-friedman: Milton Friedman (1912–2006) was an American economist, Nobel laureate, and leader of the Chicago school of free-market economics. In business ethics he is known for the 'Friedman doctrine': that a corporation's sole social responsibility is to increase its profits within the rules of the game — a provocative claim that later stakeholder and CSR debates still define themselves against.
nagarjuna: Nagarjuna (c. 150–250 AD) was an Indian Buddhist monk and philosopher, founder of the Madhyamaka ('Middle Way') school and arguably the most influential thinker in Mahayana Buddhism. He argued that everything is empty (sunyata) — lacking independent, self-contained existence — using ruthless dialectical arguments to dissolve all fixed views without asserting any.
plutarch: Plutarch (c. 46–119 AD) was a Greek Platonist best known for his Parallel Lives, biographies pairing Greek and Roman statesmen that shaped moral writing for centuries. He also wrote essays on virtue, religion, and the soul, and it is in his Life of Theseus that the Ship of Theseus puzzle about identity through change first appears.
regan: Tom Regan (1938–2017) was an American philosopher who gave the animal rights movement its leading rights-based theory. Against utilitarian approaches like Peter Singer's, he argued in The Case for Animal Rights that animals are 'subjects-of-a-life' with inherent value, so they may not be used merely as means, whatever the consequences.
tillich: Paul Tillich (1886–1965) was a German-American Protestant theologian and philosopher who tried to translate Christian faith into the language of existentialism. He described God not as a being among beings but as 'the ground of being' itself, and defined faith as 'ultimate concern' — what one stakes one's whole existence on.
tolstoy: Leo Tolstoy (1828–1910) was the great Russian novelist of War and Peace and Anna Karenina, and in later life a radical Christian moralist. He renounced violence, property, and institutional church alike, developing an ethic of nonresistance to evil that deeply influenced Gandhi and, through him, the theory of nonviolent civil disobedience.
vann-inwagen: Peter van Inwagen (b. 1942) is an American analytic metaphysician at Notre Dame, and a Christian. His Essay on Free Will made the case for incompatibilism — that free will and determinism cannot both be true — and he is known too for a starkly simple answer to the problem of evil: no argument against God's existence has been successful.
vico: Giambattista Vico (1668–1744) was a Neapolitan philosopher who challenged Descartes' model of certain knowledge, arguing that we truly understand only what we ourselves have made — above all, history and institutions. His New Science pioneered a philosophy of history in which cultures cycle through ages of gods, heroes, and human beings.
